newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Asset-backed issuance to grow in Asia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asset-backed issuance to grow in Asia.

text.p: Asia-Pacific markets promise to offer the next potentially active venue for asset-backed securities.
A relatively new financing tool, asset-backed securities (ABS) are pools of credit card receivables or auto loans bundled into a bond offering.
Assets with predictable cash flows have been securitized in the U.S. and Europe; issuance of ABS has grown in these two markets as has investor acceptance.

A group of business leaders, serving as advisors to Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), will meet this week with Asian Pacific finance ministers, central bankers and businessmen to tutor them on the mechanics of asset-backed securitization.

Founded in 1989, APEC includes 18 Asian Pacific nations which are looking to foster and encourage their economic interdependence. A 1991 charter, the Seoul APEC Declaration, identifies APEC's priorities: to sustain growth and development of the region and reduce barriers to trade.

This week's four-day visit with finance ministers and potential issuers of ABS in Manila, Jakarta, Bangkok and Seoul is viewed as a roadshow trumpeting the benefits of a financing structure little used in the Asia Pacific.
HONG KONG, INDONESIA OFFER FOOTHOLD FOR ABS

To date, a Hong Kong issuer has pooled residential mortgages into bonds, and in Indonesia there has been a credit card ABS offering. Also, future receivables on airplane tickets were securitized by a Phillipines airline, and in Thailand an auto loan transaction totaling $393 million was completed.
Assets that can be securitized include export receivables, mortgages and credit cards as well as auto loans, according to APEC presentation materials to be offered this week.

Possible issuers of ABS include commercial and consumer lenders and infrastructure developers, according to Paul Jablansky, a director at Salomon Brothers Inc, a unit of Salomon Inc, who is among those advising APEC. Jablansky will participate in this week's series of meetings.
A WIDE RANGE OF ASSETS TO BE SECURITIZED

According to APEC's presentation materials, non-mortgage assets have become a large component of the ABS market. Credit card receivables, auto loans and home equity loans accounted for most of the assets to be securitized as of June 1997.

This week's series of meetings will offer bankers an understanding of the potential offered by ABS, said Jeffrey Shafer, a vice chairman of Salomon Brothers International, who also will join in the series of presentations. Shafer is a former undersecretary for International Affairs at the U.S. Treasury.
Both Salomon Brothers executives see small- to medium-sized businesses benefitting from securitization.
But, they noted, the success of the ABS market in Asia Pacific hinges on the clarification of regulatory issues.
"International accounting standards are the key to opening markets and the finance ministers of these nations realize this," Shafer told Reuters in an interview.
LOCAL CAPITAL MARKETS: KEY TO DEVELOPMENT OF ABS MART
Asset-backed transactions can be denominated in local currencies, domestic offerings, or they can be denominated in U.S. dollars. But, domestic deals call for a key ingredient.
"For domestic deals, there is a need for a local capital market to be developed to support the market for ABS," said Jablansky.
The absence of such capital markets has resulted in a tendency to structure offshore ABS deals as U.S. dollar-denominated transactions.

Jablansky said that domestic ABS offerings were less likely to be seen in the early Asian Pacific ABS market. What was more likely were Eurobond deals and 144a private placement transactions, he said.

Eurobonds are denominated in U.S. dollars or other currencies and sold to investors outside the country whose currency is used. The Securities and Exchange Commission's rule 144a allows a non-exclusive safe harbor from registration requirements for resale to certain institutional investors of privately placed securities that are not of a class of securities listed on a U.S. exchange.

U.S. first-time issuers may have to allocate six to nine months to bring an ABS issue to market. Meanwhile, "in Asia Pacific, a new issuer would take at least that amount of time and perhaps more," said Jablansky.

In the U.S., Government-Sponsored Enterprises (GSE)-- the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp and the Federal National Mortgage Association -- have been crucial in the development of the mortgage-backed securities market.
The GSEs, which are government-sponsored businesses, buy loans from lenders and these loans are then securitized for sale into the capital markets.

Some Asian Pacific nations have a GSE-like entity, according to Jablansky and Shafer, who note that while the creation of such a GSE is not necessary, many nations want to follow the U.S. model. "Hong Kong just set one up," said Shafer.
THE CURRENCY SWAP AND AVERAGE LIVES

When it comes to the structuring of the deals, Jablansky said there likely will be domestic and offshore ABS transactions. The offshore deals, he said, have shorter average lives -- about five years and under.
The average life of the offshore deals depends on the cash flow characteristic of the asset being securitized as well as the existence of a currency swap market, said Jablansky.

The hurdle limiting a deal's average life was overcome in Hong Kong where an ABS offering had two classes. One tranche, or piece of the security, was denominated in U.S. dollars, while the other was denominated in Hong Kong dollars.

"That's how one issuer solved the problem of not having a swap market that would allow the structure to convert cashflows in the local currency to cashflows into an overseas currency," Jablansky said.
Having a dollar-denominated structure, he added, ensures that the offering enjoys a larger investor base.
Jablansky said that while much of the current ABS investor base was made up of U.S. and European investors, some local pension funds and insurers may buy the Asia Pacific ABS.

The group of ABS emissaries was sure to be closely listened to by members of the Asian-Pacific business community which includes finance ministers and central bankers anxious to diversify their source of funds.
"One of the ongoing concerns of finance ministers is how to bring in long-term debt. They want to stop using money from central banks to finance infrastructure projects," said Shafer.
((-- U.S. Mortgage Unit, 212-859-1668))
